visual.caption: Oxidation is loss of electrons; reduction is gain.

slides.narration: Burning, rusting, and the cells that power a torch all depend on the transfer of electrons from one substance to another. In this part we meet the language for describing that transfer: oxidation, reduction, and a counting scheme called the oxidation number.

slides.heading: Oxygen and hydrogen view
slides.body_md: The older definitions: **oxidation** is the **gain of oxygen** or the **loss of hydrogen**; **reduction** is the **loss of oxygen** or the **gain of hydrogen**. Addition of an electronegative element is oxidation; addition of an electropositive element is reduction.

visual.alt: Table of oxidation and reduction defined as gain or loss of oxygen or hydrogen with examples

slides.narration: Early chemists defined oxidation as the gain of oxygen or the loss of hydrogen, and reduction as the opposite. Magnesium burning in air gains oxygen, so it is oxidised. Iron oxide heated with carbon monoxide loses oxygen, so it is reduced. These ideas work but they are limited to reactions with oxygen or hydrogen.

slides.heading: The electron view and the two agents
slides.body_md: **Oxidation** is the **loss of electrons**; **reduction** is the **gain of electrons**. They occur together, so the reaction is a **redox** reaction. The substance that **gains** electrons (is reduced) is the **oxidising agent**; the one that **loses** electrons (is oxidised) is the **reducing agent**. Examples: $\ce{Fe^2+ -> Fe^3+ + e-}$ and $\ce{Cu -> Cu^2+ + 2e-}$.

visual.alt: Table linking oxidation and reduction with electrons, agent role and oxidation number

slides.narration: The modern definition is about electrons. Oxidation is loss of electrons and reduction is gain. They always happen together. The substance that is reduced takes electrons, so it is the oxidising agent. The substance that is oxidised gives electrons, so it is the reducing agent. Remember it this way: the agent is named by what it does to the other substance.

slides.heading: Worked example: name the agents
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** For each reaction, say what is oxidised and reduced and name the agents. (i) $\ce{2Na + Cl2 -> 2NaCl}$ (ii) $\ce{Cl2 + 2KI -> 2KCl + I2}$

(i) Na loses an electron, $\ce{Na -> Na+}$: Na is oxidised, a reducing agent. $\ce{Cl2}$ gains electrons, $\ce{Cl2 + 2e- -> 2Cl-}$: reduced, an oxidising agent.

(ii) $\ce{I-}$ loses an electron to give $\ce{I2}$: iodide is oxidised, the reducing agent. $\ce{Cl2}$ is reduced to $\ce{Cl-}$, the oxidising agent.

visual.alt: Table of the substance oxidised and reduced and the agents in two reactions

slides.narration: In the first reaction sodium gives up an electron, so sodium is oxidised and acts as the reducing agent. Chlorine takes the electrons, so it is reduced and is the oxidising agent. In the second reaction the same chlorine takes electrons from iodide ions, so iodide is oxidised and chlorine is again the oxidising agent.

slides.body_md: Decide which species gains electrons and which loses them.

slides.heading: Oxidation number: the idea and the rules
slides.body_md: The **oxidation number (ON)** is the charge an atom would have if all shared electrons were given to the **more electronegative** atom. It lets us follow electrons even in covalent compounds.

rows: ON of an atom in an element is 0 (Na, O₂, S₈, P₄)
ON of a monatomic ion equals its charge (Cu²⁺ is +2)
Sum of ON in a neutral compound is 0; in an ion it equals the charge
Group 1 is +1, group 2 is +2, fluorine is −1 always
H is +1 (−1 in metal hydrides); O is −2 (−1 in peroxides, +2 in OF₂)

visual.alt: Table of the five rules for assigning oxidation numbers

slides.narration: The oxidation number is the charge an atom would carry if the bonding electrons went entirely to the more electronegative atom. Five rules let us assign it. Atoms in elements are zero. Simple ions carry their charge. The numbers add up to the overall charge. Alkali metals are plus one, fluorine is minus one, and hydrogen and oxygen have the usual values plus one and minus two.

slides.heading: Exceptions, and fractional oxidation numbers
slides.body_md: Hydrogen is **−1** in hydrides ($\ce{NaH}$, $\ce{CaH2}$). Oxygen is **−1** in peroxides ($\ce{H2O2}$) and **+2** in $\ce{OF2}$. An **average** ON can be fractional, e.g. S in $\ce{Na2S4O6}$ is $+2.5$: it is an **average** of atoms with different actual numbers. Fluorine never shows a positive ON.

visual.alt: Table of exceptional and fractional oxidation numbers with reasons

slides.narration: Some atoms break the usual pattern. Hydrogen is minus one when it is joined to a metal. Oxygen is minus one in peroxides. In oxygen difluoride oxygen is plus two, because fluorine is the most electronegative element. An average oxidation number can be a fraction, which only means that different atoms of the same element have different actual numbers.

slides.heading: Chlorine across its oxidation states
slides.body_md: Chlorine shows ON from **−1 to +7**. Moving **right** on the line is oxidation; moving **left** is reduction. A species at the top of the range (ClO₄⁻) can only be **reduced**; one at the bottom (Cl⁻) can only be **oxidised**; intermediate ones can do both.

slides.heading: Redox as a change in oxidation number
slides.body_md: A reaction is a **redox reaction** if the ON of at least one element **changes**. **Oxidation** is an **increase** in ON; **reduction** is a **decrease**. The **total increase** equals the **total decrease**. If no ON changes, the reaction is not redox (precipitation, neutralisation).

visual.alt: Table of four reactions with oxidation number changes and whether each is redox

slides.narration: Count the oxidation numbers on both sides. If at least one element changes, the reaction is redox. The element that goes up is oxidised, the one that goes down is reduced, and the total rise equals the total fall. Precipitation and neutralisation reactions leave every oxidation number unchanged, so they are not redox.

slides.heading: Worked example: is it redox?
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Use ON to decide which reactions are redox, and name the oxidising agent where they are.

(i) $\ce{2KI + Cl2 -> 2KCl + I2}$: I: $-1 \to 0$ (oxidised); Cl: $0 \to -1$ (reduced). **Redox**; Cl₂ is the oxidising agent.

(ii) $\ce{BaCl2 + Na2SO4 -> BaSO4 + 2NaCl}$: Ba +2, Cl −1, Na +1, S +6 on both sides. **Not redox**.

(iii) $\ce{Fe2O3 + 3CO -> 2Fe + 3CO2}$: Fe $+3 \to 0$; C $+2 \to +4$. **Redox**; Fe₂O₃ is the oxidising agent and CO the reducing agent.

visual.alt: Table of three reactions with the element oxidised, reduced and whether each is redox

slides.narration: In the first reaction iodine rises and chlorine falls, so it is redox. In the second, barium sulphate precipitates, but every oxidation number is the same on both sides, so it is not redox. In the third, iron falls from plus three to zero and carbon rises from plus two to plus four, so iron oxide is the oxidising agent.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 1
bullets: Oxidation: gain of oxygen, loss of hydrogen, loss of electrons, increase in ON. Reduction is the reverse.
Oxidising agent: gains electrons, is reduced, its ON falls. Reducing agent: loses electrons, is oxidised, its ON rises.
ON rules: element 0; monatomic ion = charge; sum = charge of species; F −1; H +1 (−1 in hydrides); O −2 (−1 in peroxides).
K₂Cr₂O₇: Cr +6; S₂O₃²⁻: S +2. Average ON may be fractional.
A reaction is redox if any ON changes; total rise = total fall.

visual.alt: Summary table of the redox meaning of changes in oxidation number

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part One. Oxidation is loss of electrons and a rise in oxidation number. Reduction is gain and a fall. The oxidising agent is reduced and the reducing agent is oxidised. We assign oxidation numbers with a small set of rules, and a reaction is redox only if some oxidation number changes.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 1
bullets: Show the sum equation when calculating an ON: sum equals the charge of the species, not always zero.
Name the agent by what it does: the oxidising agent is the species that is reduced.
Always write the sign with an ON (+6, −1) and say "average" for fractional values.
Justify "redox" by quoting the ON before and after for the element that changes.
Peroxides (O −1), OF₂ (O +2) and hydrides (H −1) are favourite exceptions.

rows: Calling the species that is oxidised the oxidising agent
Setting the sum to 0 for an ion
Set it equal to the ion charge

visual.alt: Table of common slips in Part 1 and their fixes

slides.narration: Some exam tips for Part One. Show the sum equation for any oxidation number. Remember that the oxidising agent is the species that is itself reduced. Always write the sign. Quote the before and after oxidation numbers to prove a reaction is redox. And watch for peroxides, hydrides and oxygen difluoride.

slides.heading: Balancing redox equations
slides.body_md: Part 2: a balanced redox equation must conserve **atoms and charge**, and the **electrons lost must equal the electrons gained**. Two systematic methods do this. Then we classify redox reactions.

visual.alt: Flow chart from a skeletal equation through two balancing methods to the check and the types of redox reaction

slides.narration: In this part we learn to balance redox equations, which are often too complicated for trial and error. We study two methods. One uses oxidation numbers and the other uses half reactions with electrons. Either way, we finish by checking that both atoms and charge are balanced. Then we classify redox reactions into four types.

slides.heading: The oxidation number method: steps
slides.body_md: Start from the **skeletal** (unbalanced) equation.

nodes.label: 2. Assign ON; find the atoms that change
3. Find the rise and fall per atom
4. Multiply to make total rise equal total fall
5. Balance other atoms; O with H2O, H with H+

visual.alt: Flow chart of the six steps of the oxidation number method

slides.narration: The oxidation number method has six steps. Write the skeletal equation. Assign oxidation numbers and find which atoms change. Work out the rise and the fall for each. Multiply so that the total rise equals the total fall. Balance the remaining atoms, oxygen with water and hydrogen with hydrogen ions. Finally check both atoms and charge.

slides.narration: In this skeletal equation manganese falls from plus seven to plus two, a fall of five. Iron rises from plus two to plus three, a rise of one. To make the total rise equal the total fall, five iron ions are needed for every one permanganate ion. This fixes the ratio before we balance anything else.

slides.heading: Worked example: permanganate and iron(II), oxidation number method
slides.body_md:
**Skeletal equation (acidic medium):** $\ce{MnO4- + Fe^2+ -> Mn^2+ + Fe^3+}$

1. ON: Mn $+7 \to +2$ (fall 5); Fe $+2 \to +3$ (rise 1).
2. Multiply $\ce{Fe^2+}$ and $\ce{Fe^3+}$ by 5: $\ce{MnO4- + 5Fe^2+ -> Mn^2+ + 5Fe^3+}$.
3. Charge: left $-1 + 10 = +9$, right $+2 + 15 = +17$. Add $8\ \ce{H+}$ to the left in acidic medium.
4. Balance O: 4 O on the left, so $4\ \ce{H2O}$ on the right; H now balances (8 each).

$\ce{MnO4- + 8H+ + 5Fe^2+ -> Mn^2+ + 4H2O + 5Fe^3+}$ Check: atoms Mn 1, O 4, H 8, Fe 5; charge $+17$ on each side.

visual.alt: Table checking atoms and charge of the balanced permanganate iron(II) equation

slides.narration: Start by finding the rise and fall. Multiply the iron species by five. Then compare the charges. The left side has plus nine and the right side plus seventeen, so add eight hydrogen ions to the left in acidic solution. The oxygen on the left then needs four water molecules on the right, which also balances the hydrogen. Check atoms and charge at the end.

slides.body_md: Split the skeletal equation into an **oxidation half** and a **reduction half** and balance each separately.

nodes.label: 2. Balance atoms other than O and H
6. Multiply to equalise electrons, add, cancel
7. Basic medium: add OH- to turn H+ into H2O

slides.narration: The ion electron method balances each half reaction on its own. Balance the main atoms, then oxygen with water, then hydrogen with hydrogen ions, then charge with electrons. Multiply the halves so the electrons are equal, add, and cancel. In basic solution there is one extra step, where hydroxide ions are added to turn the hydrogen ions into water.

slides.body_md: The oxidation half $\ce{Fe^2+ -> Fe^3+ + e-}$ is multiplied by 5; the reduction half takes in the 5 electrons. Adding gives the same equation as before.

Those five electrons are taken up by permanganate with eight hydrogen ions to form manganese two plus and four water molecules. Add the halves, the electrons cancel, and the balanced equation appears.

slides.heading: Worked example: dichromate and iron(II), ion-electron method
slides.body_md:
**Skeletal:** $\ce{Cr2O7^2- + Fe^2+ -> Cr^3+ + Fe^3+}$ (acidic medium).

Oxidation: $\ce{Fe^2+ -> Fe^3+ + e-}$. Reduction: $\ce{Cr2O7^2- -> 2Cr^3+}$; O: $+7\ \ce{H2O}$; H: $+14\ \ce{H+}$; charge: $+6\ \ce{e-}$, giving $\ce{Cr2O7^2- + 14H+ + 6e- -> 2Cr^3+ + 7H2O}$.

Multiply the oxidation half by 6 and add: $\ce{Cr2O7^2- + 14H+ + 6Fe^2+ -> 2Cr^3+ + 7H2O + 6Fe^3+}$ Charge: $-2 + 14 + 12 = +24$ and $2(+3) + 6(+3) = +24$.

visual.alt: Table checking atoms and charge of the balanced dichromate iron(II) equation

slides.narration: In the reduction half, dichromate gives two chromium three plus ions. Seven oxygens need seven waters on the right, which needs fourteen hydrogen ions on the left. The charge on the left is then plus twelve and on the right plus six, so six electrons are added to the left. Multiply the iron half by six, add, and the electrons cancel.

slides.heading: Basic medium
slides.body_md: In basic medium balance **as if acidic**, then add as many $\ce{OH-}$ to **both sides** as there are $\ce{H+}$, turn $\ce{H+ + OH-}$ into $\ce{H2O}$ and cancel any water that appears on both sides. Or balance O with $\ce{H2O}$ and H with $\ce{OH-}$ directly in each half.

visual.alt: Table comparing the species used to balance oxygen and hydrogen in acidic and basic media

slides.narration: In basic solution there are no free hydrogen ions to use. One route is to balance as if the solution were acidic, then add hydroxide ions to both sides to turn every hydrogen ion into water. Cancel any water that appears on both sides. The final equation then contains hydroxide ions, not hydrogen ions.

slides.heading: Worked example: basic medium, two methods
slides.body_md:
**(a) Ion-electron.** Skeletal: $\ce{CrO2- + H2O2 -> CrO4^2-}$ (basic). Oxidation: $\ce{CrO2- + 4OH- -> CrO4^2- + 2H2O + 3e-}$. Reduction: $\ce{H2O2 + 2e- -> 2OH-}$. Multiply by 2 and 3 (6 electrons): $\ce{2CrO2- + 3H2O2 + 2OH- -> 2CrO4^2- + 4H2O}$

**(b) ON method.** Skeletal: $\ce{MnO4- + I- -> MnO2 + I2}$. Mn $+7 \to +4$ (fall 3 per Mn); I $-1 \to 0$ (rise 1 per I). Total fall = total rise: $1 \times 3 = 3 \times 1$, so 2 MnO₄⁻ need 6 I⁻. Balance O with H₂O and H with OH⁻: $\ce{2MnO4- + 6I- + 4H2O -> 2MnO2 + 3I2 + 8OH-}$ Atoms balance, and charge is $-8$ on each side.

visual.alt: Table of two balanced reactions in basic medium with method and electrons transferred

slides.narration: In the first example, chromium rises from plus three to plus six in each ion, and hydrogen peroxide takes the electrons. Multiply the halves by two and three so that six electrons are shared. In the second, manganese falls by three and iodide rises by one, so six iodide ions are needed for two permanganate ions. The result contains hydroxide ions.

slides.body_md: Where do hydroxide ions appear?
slides.narration: Quick check. Think about which species are available in basic solution and which side of the equation the hydroxide ions finally appear on. Then check how your chosen equation balances in atoms and in charge before you pick an answer.

slides.heading: Types of redox reaction
slides.body_md: **Combination:** two or more substances form one ($\ce{2Na + Cl2 -> 2NaCl}$). **Decomposition:** one compound gives two or more, redox if an element changes ON ($\ce{2HgO -> 2Hg + O2}$). **Displacement:** a more reactive element displaces a less reactive one ($\ce{Cl2 + 2KI -> 2KCl + I2}$). **Disproportionation:** one element is **simultaneously oxidised and reduced**.

slides.narration: Redox reactions fall into four types. In combination, substances unite, with at least one element involved. In decomposition, a compound breaks up, and it is redox if an element changes its oxidation number. In displacement a more reactive element takes the place of a less reactive one. In disproportionation, one element is both oxidised and reduced in the same reaction.

The same element goes down and up in one reaction, which is disproportionation. It only occurs when the element has an oxidation number in the middle of its range, so that it can move either way.

slides.heading: Worked example: classify and balance
slides.body_md:
**(i)** $\ce{3Cl2 + 6OH- -> 5Cl- + ClO3- + 3H2O}$: Cl $0 \to -1$ and $0 \to +5$: **disproportionation**.

**(ii)** $\ce{2KClO3 -> 2KCl + 3O2}$: Cl $+5 \to -1$, O $-2 \to 0$: **decomposition** (redox).

**(iii)** $\ce{Fe + Cu^2+ -> Fe^2+ + Cu}$: Fe $0 \to +2$, Cu $+2 \to 0$: **displacement**.

**(iv)** Skeletal: $\ce{S2O3^2- + Cl2 + H2O -> SO4^2- + Cl- + H+}$. S: $+2 \to +6$ (rise 4 per S, 8 per $\ce{S2O3^2-}$); Cl: $0 \to -1$ (fall 2 per $\ce{Cl2}$): 4 Cl₂ per thiosulphate. $\ce{S2O3^2- + 4Cl2 + 5H2O -> 2SO4^2- + 8Cl- + 10H+}$

slides.narration: Always look for the evidence in the oxidation numbers. Chlorine going both down and up in one reaction is disproportionation. Potassium chlorate breaking into chloride and oxygen is decomposition, and it is redox, because chlorine and oxygen both change. Iron pushing copper out of solution is displacement. The thiosulphate and chlorine equation shows the ON method with a larger multiplier.

sections.heading: 1. Oxidation and reduction; oxidising and reducing agents
sections.body_md:
| Definition | Oxidation | Reduction |
|---|---|---|
| Oxygen | gain of oxygen | loss of oxygen |
| Hydrogen | loss of hydrogen | gain of hydrogen |
| Electrons | **loss** of electrons | **gain** of electrons |
| Oxidation number | increases | decreases |

The two always occur **together** (redox). The substance that **gains** electrons is reduced and is the **oxidising agent**; the substance that **loses** electrons is oxidised and is the **reducing agent**. Examples: $\ce{2Na + Cl2 -> 2NaCl}$ (Na reducing agent, Cl₂ oxidising agent); $\ce{Fe2O3 + 3CO -> 2Fe + 3CO2}$ (CO is the reducing agent, Fe₂O₃ the oxidising agent).

Gain of electrons, loss of oxygen, gain of hydrogen; a decrease in oxidation number.
The substance that gains electrons (is reduced) and so oxidises the other substance.
The substance that loses electrons (is oxidised) and so reduces the other substance.

sections.heading: 2. Oxidation number: the rules
sections.body_md:
The **oxidation number (ON)** is the charge an atom would have if all bonding electrons were assigned to the more electronegative atom.

1. ON of an atom in an **element** is 0.
2. ON of a **monatomic ion** equals its charge.
3. The **sum** of ON in a neutral compound is 0; in a polyatomic ion it equals the ion's charge.
4. Group 1 metals are +1, group 2 metals +2, **fluorine −1** always.
5. **Hydrogen +1** (−1 in metal hydrides such as NaH, CaH₂). **Oxygen −2** (−1 in peroxides such as H₂O₂, +2 in OF₂, −½ in superoxides).

The ON can be **fractional** when it is an **average** over atoms of the same element (S in Na₂S₄O₆, Fe in Fe₃O₄).

key_terms.definition_md: The charge an atom would carry if the shared electrons were given to the more electronegative atom.
The mean value for atoms of one element in a species where they are not all identical; it may be a fraction.

sections.heading: 3. Calculating oxidation numbers; redox as a change in oxidation number
sections.body_md:
Write one equation: (sum of ON of all atoms) $=$ charge of the species.

- $\ce{K2Cr2O7}$: $2(+1) + 2x + 7(-2) = 0$, so Cr $= +6$.
- $\ce{S2O3^2-}$: $2x + 3(-2) = -2$, so S $= +2$.
- $\ce{MnO4-}$: $x - 8 = -1$, so Mn $= +7$; $\ce{MnO4^2-}$: Mn $= +6$.

A reaction is **redox** if the ON of some element **changes**; oxidation is an **increase** and reduction a **decrease**, and the **total increase equals the total decrease**. Precipitation and neutralisation are **not** redox.

key_terms.definition_md: A reaction in which the oxidation number of at least one element changes.

sections.heading: 4. Balancing by the oxidation number method
sections.body_md:
1. Write the **skeletal** equation. 2. Assign ON and find the atoms that change. 3. Find the **rise** and **fall** per atom. 4. Multiply so that **total rise = total fall**. 5. Balance the remaining atoms: **O with H₂O, H with H⁺** (acidic; with OH⁻ in basic). 6. Check **atoms and charge**.

Worked: $\ce{MnO4- + Fe^2+ -> Mn^2+ + Fe^3+}$ (skeletal). Mn falls by 5, Fe rises by 1: use 5 Fe²⁺. Charge left $-1 + 10 = +9$, right $+17$: add 8 H⁺ on the left; then 4 H₂O on the right. $\ce{MnO4- + 8H+ + 5Fe^2+ -> Mn^2+ + 4H2O + 5Fe^3+}$

Also: $\ce{3Cu + 2NO3- + 8H+ -> 3Cu^2+ + 2NO + 4H2O}$ (Cu 0 → +2, N +5 → +2, 3 Cu per 2 NO₃⁻).

sections.heading: 5. Balancing by the ion-electron method; acidic and basic media
sections.body_md:
Split into **oxidation** and **reduction** half-reactions. In each: balance atoms other than O and H; **O with H₂O**; **H with H⁺**; **charge with electrons**. Multiply to equalise electrons, add and cancel.

Acidic: $\ce{MnO4- + 8H+ + 5e- -> Mn^2+ + 4H2O}$ and $\ce{Fe^2+ -> Fe^3+ + e-}$ (×5) give $\ce{MnO4- + 8H+ + 5Fe^2+ -> Mn^2+ + 4H2O + 5Fe^3+}$ Also $\ce{Cr2O7^2- + 14H+ + 6e- -> 2Cr^3+ + 7H2O}$ gives $\ce{Cr2O7^2- + 14H+ + 6Fe^2+ -> 2Cr^3+ + 7H2O + 6Fe^3+}$

**Basic medium:** after balancing as if acidic, add OH⁻ to both sides equal to the number of H⁺, form H₂O and cancel. Example: $\ce{2CrO2- + 3H2O2 + 2OH- -> 2CrO4^2- + 4H2O}$ Always check atoms **and** charge.

sections.heading: 6. Types of redox reaction and applications
sections.body_md:
- **Combination:** $\ce{2Na + Cl2 -> 2NaCl}$.
- **Decomposition** (redox when an element changes ON): $\ce{2KClO3 -> 2KCl + 3O2}$; $\ce{2HgO -> 2Hg + O2}$.
- **Displacement:** $\ce{Cl2 + 2KI -> 2KCl + I2}$; $\ce{Zn + 2H+ -> Zn^2+ + H2}$; $\ce{Fe + Cu^2+ -> Fe^2+ + Cu}$.
- **Disproportionation:** one element is simultaneously oxidised and reduced, so it must be in an **intermediate ON**: $\ce{Cl2 + 2OH- -> Cl- + ClO- + H2O}$ and $\ce{3Cl2 + 6OH- -> 5Cl- + ClO3- + 3H2O}$.

**Applications:** the same ideas explain combustion, rusting, extraction of metals (reduction of ores), bleaching, and the titration of Fe²⁺ with permanganate or dichromate in acid.

key_terms.definition_md: A reaction in which a more reactive element displaces a less reactive one from its compound.
A redox reaction in which the same element is both oxidised and reduced.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Naming the species that is oxidised as the oxidising agent.
- Setting the sum of oxidation numbers to 0 for an ion.
- Balancing atoms but forgetting charge; leaving H⁺ in a basic-medium equation.
- Taking O as −2 in peroxides and OF₂.
- Saying "disproportionation" without showing one element going both up and down.
**Marks**
- Oxidation number: equation (1), answer with sign (1).
- Balancing: ON change or half-reactions (1), multipliers (1), balanced equation (1), check of atoms and charge (1).
- Classification: ON evidence (1), type (1).

cards.front_md: Oxidation in terms of oxygen, hydrogen and electrons?
cards.back_md: Gain of oxygen, loss of hydrogen, loss of electrons.

cards.front_md: Reduction in terms of oxygen, hydrogen and electrons?
cards.back_md: Loss of oxygen, gain of hydrogen, gain of electrons.

cards.front_md: What is a redox reaction?
cards.back_md: A reaction in which oxidation and reduction occur together.

cards.front_md: What is an oxidising agent?
cards.back_md: The substance that gains electrons and is itself reduced.

cards.front_md: What is a reducing agent?
cards.back_md: The substance that loses electrons and is itself oxidised.

cards.front_md: In 2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl name the agents.
cards.back_md: Na is the reducing agent; Cl₂ is the oxidising agent.

cards.front_md: In Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂ which is reduced?
cards.back_md: Fe₂O₃ (iron falls from +3 to 0); CO is oxidised.

cards.front_md: Define oxidation number.
cards.back_md: The charge an atom would have if all bonding electrons went to the more electronegative atom.

cards.front_md: ON of an atom in an element?
cards.back_md: Zero (Na, O₂, S₈, P₄).

cards.front_md: Sum of ON in a neutral compound and in an ion?
cards.back_md: Zero for a neutral compound; equal to the charge for an ion.

cards.front_md: ON of fluorine?
cards.back_md: Always −1 in compounds.

cards.front_md: Usual ON of hydrogen and its exception?
cards.back_md: +1; −1 in metal hydrides such as NaH.

cards.front_md: Usual ON of oxygen and its exceptions?
cards.back_md: −2; −1 in peroxides; +2 in OF₂.

cards.front_md: ON of Cr in K₂Cr₂O₇?
ON of S in S₂O₃²⁻?
ON of Mn in KMnO₄ and in K₂MnO₄?
Why can an ON be fractional?
cards.back_md: It is an average over atoms of the same element with different actual numbers, as S in Na₂S₄O₆ (+2.5).

cards.front_md: How does ON show oxidation and reduction?
cards.back_md: Oxidation: ON increases. Reduction: ON decreases. Total rise = total fall.

cards.front_md: Is a precipitation reaction redox?
cards.back_md: No: no oxidation number changes.

cards.front_md: Steps of the oxidation number method?
cards.back_md: Skeletal equation; ON; rise and fall; equalise; balance O, H; check atoms and charge.

cards.front_md: In MnO₄⁻ → Mn²⁺ how much does the ON of Mn change?
cards.back_md: It falls by 5 (+7 to +2), so 5 Fe²⁺ (rise 1 each) are needed.

cards.front_md: Balanced equation of MnO₄⁻ with Fe²⁺ in acid?
cards.back_md: MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5Fe²⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O + 5Fe³⁺.

cards.front_md: How many electrons does Cr₂O₇²⁻ gain in acid?
cards.back_md: Six: Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 14H⁺ + 6e⁻ → 2Cr³⁺ + 7H₂O.

cards.front_md: Steps of the ion-electron method?
cards.back_md: Two half-reactions; balance atoms, O with H₂O, H with H⁺, charge with e⁻; equalise electrons; add.

cards.front_md: Which side do electrons appear on in a reduction half?
cards.back_md: On the left (reactant side); in an oxidation half they are on the right.

cards.front_md: How is a basic-medium equation balanced?
cards.back_md: Balance as in acid, add OH⁻ to both sides to turn H⁺ into H₂O, and cancel water.

cards.front_md: What must be checked in a balanced redox equation?
cards.back_md: Atoms of every element and the total charge on each side.

cards.front_md: Name the four types of redox reaction.
cards.back_md: Combination, decomposition, displacement, disproportionation.

cards.front_md: Define disproportionation with an example.
cards.back_md: One element is simultaneously oxidised and reduced: Cl₂ + 2OH⁻ → Cl⁻ + ClO⁻ + H₂O.

cards.front_md: When is a decomposition reaction redox?
cards.back_md: When an element changes its oxidation number, e.g. 2KClO₃ → 2KCl + 3O₂ but not CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂.

cards.front_md: What condition lets an element disproportionate?
cards.back_md: It must be in an intermediate oxidation number so that it can both rise and fall.

questions.stem_md: A railway workshop welds broken tracks with the thermite mixture. The reaction is $\ce{2Al + Fe2O3 -> Al2O3 + 2Fe}$. Which statement is correct?

options.text_md: Aluminium is the oxidising agent, because it gains oxygen
Aluminium is the reducing agent, because it loses electrons and is oxidised
Iron(III) oxide is the reducing agent, because it loses oxygen
Both aluminium and iron are reduced

questions.solution_md: Al goes from 0 to $+3$ (oxidised), so it is the reducing agent; Fe goes from $+3$ to 0 (reduced), so $\ce{Fe2O3}$ is the oxidising agent — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Which of the following changes of a species, written as a half-reaction, is an oxidation?

options.text_md: S²⁻ → S + 2e⁻
Cl₂ + 2e⁻ → 2Cl⁻
Fe³⁺ + e⁻ → Fe²⁺
Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu

questions.solution_md: Oxidation is loss of electrons, with electrons on the right-hand side: S²⁻ loses 2 electrons (ON −2 to 0). The others gain electrons and are reductions — option (a).

questions.stem_md: In a gas-works the reaction $\ce{H2S + Cl2 -> 2HCl + S}$ is used to remove sulphur compounds. Which species is the reducing agent?

options.text_md: H₂S, because sulphur rises from −2 to 0
Cl₂, because chlorine rises from 0 to −1
HCl, because it is a product
S, because it is a solid product

questions.solution_md: In $\ce{H2S}$, S is $-2$ and in the product S is 0: it loses electrons, so $\ce{H2S}$ is oxidised and is the reducing agent; chlorine goes from 0 to $-1$ and is reduced — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A strip of iron of mass 2.8 g (M = 56 g mol⁻¹) is completely oxidised to Fe³⁺ ions by an excess of an oxidising agent. The amount of electrons lost by the iron is:

options.text_md: 0.05 mol
0.10 mol
8.40 mol
0.15 mol

questions.solution_md: Moles of Fe $= 2.8/56 = 0.05$; each Fe loses 3 electrons ($\ce{Fe -> Fe^3+ + 3e-}$), so electrons lost $= 3 \times 0.05 = 0.15$ mol — option (d).

questions.stem_md: In the Haber process $\ce{N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3}$, nitrogen is converted to ammonia. In terms of hydrogen and oxidation numbers, nitrogen is:

options.text_md: oxidised, because it gains hydrogen and its oxidation number rises
reduced, because its oxidation number rises from 0 to +3
reduced, because it gains hydrogen and its oxidation number falls from 0 to −3
neither oxidised nor reduced, because no oxygen is involved

questions.solution_md: Gain of hydrogen is reduction. In NH₃, N is −3 (3 × (+1) + x = 0), so its ON falls from 0 to −3 — option (c).

questions.stem_md: The orange crystals of potassium dichromate, K₂Cr₂O₇, are used in a school titration. The oxidation number of chromium in this compound is:
questions.solution_md: $2(+1) + 2x + 7(-2) = 0$, so $2x = +12$ and $x = +6$ — option (d). (+12 is the total for two atoms.)

questions.stem_md: A chemist in a detergent factory analyses diphosphoric acid, H₄P₂O₇. The oxidation number of phosphorus in it is:
Sodium thiosulphate, Na₂S₂O₃, is used as a photographic fixer. The oxidation number of sulphur in the thiosulphate ion, S₂O₃²⁻, is:
questions.solution_md: For the ion the sum equals the charge: $2x + 3(-2) = -2$, so $x = +2$ — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Carbon is present in methane, methanol, methanal and carbon dioxide. In methanol, CH₃OH, the oxidation number of carbon is:
A gas cooker burns methane: $\ce{CH4 + 2O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O}$. The total change in the oxidation number of carbon, and its direction, are:

options.text_md: an increase of 8, from −4 to +4
a decrease of 8, from +4 to −4
an increase of 4, from 0 to +4
no change, because carbon is tetravalent in both

questions.solution_md: In $\ce{CH4}$: $x + 4 = 0$, so C is $−4$; in $\ce{CO2}$: $x - 4 = 0$, so C is $+4$. The increase is $8$ — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Calcium hydride is used to dry solvents: $\ce{CaH2 + 2H2O -> Ca(OH)2 + 2H2}$. Which statement about this reaction is correct?

options.text_md: Water is the reducing agent, because oxygen is unchanged
CaH₂ is the oxidising agent, because hydrogen in it is +1
It is not a redox reaction, because no element changes its oxidation number
Water is the oxidising agent, because hydrogen in H₂O falls from +1 to 0

questions.solution_md: In CaH₂ hydrogen is −1 (hydride); in H₂O it is +1; in H₂ it is 0. Hydrogen in water falls from +1 to 0 (reduced, so water is the oxidising agent), while hydride rises from −1 to 0 — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A student mixes solutions of lead(II) nitrate and potassium iodide and a yellow solid forms. Which description of this reaction is correct?

options.text_md: It is a redox reaction, because a precipitate forms
It is not a redox reaction, because no oxidation number changes
It is a redox reaction, because iodide is oxidised to iodine
It is a redox reaction, because lead is reduced to the metal

questions.solution_md: $\ce{Pb(NO3)2 + 2KI -> PbI2 + 2KNO3}$: Pb stays $+2$, I stays $-1$, K $+1$, N $+5$ and O $-2$. With no change in any oxidation number the reaction is not redox — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Potassium chlorate, KClO₃, is used in safety matches. Chlorine has the same oxidation number in it as in which of the following?

options.text_md: Cl₂O₅, dichlorine pentoxide
ClO₄⁻, the perchlorate ion
ClO⁻, the hypochlorite ion
Cl₂, chlorine gas

questions.solution_md: In $\ce{KClO3}$: $+1 + x - 6 = 0$, $x = +5$. In $\ce{Cl2O5}$: $2x - 10 = 0$, so chlorine is also +5. In $\ce{ClO4-}$ chlorine is +7, in $\ce{ClO-}$ it is +1 and in $\ce{Cl2}$ it is 0 — option (a).

questions.stem_md: In the balanced ionic equation for dichromate ions oxidising iron(II) ions in acidic solution, the coefficient of H⁺ and the number of electrons gained by one Cr₂O₇²⁻ ion are, respectively:

options.text_md: 7 and 6
14 and 3
14 and 6
8 and 5

questions.solution_md: Reduction half: $\ce{Cr2O7^2- + 14H+ + 6e- -> 2Cr^3+ + 7H2O}$ — 14 H⁺ and 6 electrons (2 × (+6 to +3)) — option (c).

questions.stem_md: In the reduction of nitrate to nitrogen monoxide in acid, the skeletal half-reaction is $\ce{NO3- -> NO}$. The number of electrons appearing in the balanced half-reaction, and on which side, is:

options.text_md: 3, on the right (product) side
5, on the left (reactant) side
3, on the left (reactant) side
2, on the left (reactant) side

questions.solution_md: N goes from $+5$ to $+2$, so 3 electrons are gained: $\ce{NO3- + 4H+ + 3e- -> NO + 2H2O}$ with electrons on the left — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Permanganate is reduced to manganese dioxide by iodide in basic medium; the balanced equation is $\ce{2MnO4- + 6I- + 4H2O -> 2MnO2 + 3I2 + 8OH-}$. Which statement is correct?

options.text_md: Hydrogen ions appear on the left-hand side, with charge +8
Hydroxide ions appear on the left-hand side, with charge −8
The charge is −2 on the left and −8 on the right
The hydroxide ions appear on the right-hand side, and the charge is −8 on each side

questions.solution_md: Left: $2(-1) + 6(-1) = -8$; right: $8(-1) = -8$. Basic-medium equations contain $\ce{OH-}$, here on the product side, and no $\ce{H+}$ — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Copper dissolves in dilute nitric acid: $\ce{3Cu + 2NO3- + 8H+ -> 3Cu^2+ + 2NO + 4H2O}$. What is the ratio of the amounts of copper and nitrate ions that react, and the number of electrons transferred in all?

options.text_md: 2 : 3, with 6 electrons transferred in all
3 : 2, with 3 electrons transferred in all
3 : 2, with 6 electrons transferred in all
1 : 1, with 2 electrons transferred in all

questions.solution_md: Cu rises by 2 per atom, N falls by 3 per atom. Total rise $= 3 \times 2 = 6$, total fall $= 2 \times 3 = 6$, so the ratio Cu : $\ce{NO3-}$ is 3 : 2 and 6 electrons are transferred — option (c).

questions.stem_md: While balancing the reduction half-reaction $\ce{MnO4- -> Mn^2+}$ in acidic medium by the ion-electron method, the four oxygen atoms on the left are balanced by adding:

options.text_md: 4 OH⁻ to the left-hand side
8 H⁺ to the right-hand side
4 H₂O to the right-hand side
4 O₂ to the right-hand side

questions.solution_md: Oxygen is balanced with water in either medium: add 4 H₂O on the right, then balance the hydrogen with 8 H⁺ on the left and the charge with 5 electrons — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A mass of potassium dichromate containing 0.020 mol of Cr₂O₇²⁻ is added to an acidified iron(II) solution. The amount of Fe²⁺ that can be oxidised completely is:

options.text_md: 0.06 mol
0.12 mol
0.04 mol
0.28 mol

questions.solution_md: Each $\ce{Cr2O7^2-}$ gains 6 electrons and each $\ce{Fe^2+}$ loses 1, so $n(\ce{Fe^2+}) = 6 \times 0.020 = 0.12$ mol — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is a disproportionation reaction?

options.text_md: Cl₂ + 2NaBr → 2NaCl + Br₂
2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl
2HgO → 2Hg + O₂
Cl₂ + 2OH⁻ → Cl⁻ + ClO⁻ + H₂O

questions.solution_md: In Cl₂ + 2OH⁻ → Cl⁻ + ClO⁻ + H₂O, chlorine goes from 0 to −1 and to +1: one element is both reduced and oxidised. The others are displacement, combination and decomposition — option (d).

questions.stem_md: On heating, each of the following decomposes. Which decomposition is also a redox reaction?

options.text_md: Calcium carbonate, forming calcium oxide and carbon dioxide
Mercury(II) oxide, forming mercury and oxygen
Calcium hydroxide, forming calcium oxide and water
Ammonium chloride, forming ammonia and hydrogen chloride

questions.solution_md: $\ce{2HgO -> 2Hg + O2}$: Hg $+2 \to 0$ and O $-2 \to 0$, so oxidation numbers change. In the others every oxidation number is unchanged — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A student places strips of zinc, silver, gold and mercury (in the order of the activity series zinc > copper > mercury > silver > gold) in separate beakers of blue copper(II) sulphate solution. In which beaker does the colour fade and a red-brown solid form?

options.text_md: Zinc, because it is more reactive and displaces copper
Silver, because it is a good conductor
Gold, because it is a noble metal
Mercury, because it is a liquid metal

questions.solution_md: Only a metal above copper in the activity series displaces it: $\ce{Zn + Cu^2+ -> Zn^2+ + Cu}$ (Zn $0 \to +2$, Cu $+2 \to 0$) — option (a).

questions.stem_md: In an engine cylinder at very high temperature, nitrogen and oxygen combine: $\ce{N2 + O2 -> 2NO}$. This reaction is best described as:

options.text_md: a combination reaction that is not redox, since the elements are in their standard states
a displacement reaction, since one element replaces another
a disproportionation reaction, since both products are oxides
a combination reaction that is also redox, since N rises from 0 to +2 and O falls from 0 to −2

questions.solution_md: Two elements join to form one compound (combination), and the oxidation numbers change: N $0 \to +2$ (oxidised) and O $0 \to -2$ (reduced) — option (d).

questions.stem_md: In dilute sulphuric acid, copper(I) ions are unstable and change to copper metal and copper(II) ions: $\ce{2Cu+ -> Cu^2+ + Cu}$. This is a case of:

options.text_md: disproportionation, because Cu⁺ is both oxidised (+1 to +2) and reduced (+1 to 0)
displacement, because copper replaces copper
decomposition, because one species gives two products with no change in oxidation number
combination, because two copper species form a single product

questions.solution_md: The single species $\ce{Cu+}$ ($+1$) forms $\ce{Cu^2+}$ ($+2$, oxidised) and $\ce{Cu}$ (0, reduced): the same element rises and falls — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A zinc granule dropped into copper(II) sulphate solution is oxidised, and the blue colour fades.

**Reason (R):** The oxidation number of zinc rises from 0 to +2 while that of copper falls from +2 to 0.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both statements are true. Zinc loses electrons (ON 0 to +2) and Cu²⁺ gains them (ON +2 to 0), so the blue colour of Cu²⁺ fades; Reason explains Assertion — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Chlorine undergoes disproportionation when it reacts with cold dilute sodium hydroxide.

**Reason (R):** Chlorine gas is greenish yellow in colour and has a pungent smell.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both statements are true, but the Reason is unrelated to the Assertion: disproportionation occurs because chlorine, in an intermediate state (0), can be both oxidised (to +1) and reduced (to −1) — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The oxidation number of oxygen in oxygen difluoride, OF₂, is +2.

**Reason (R):** Oxygen is more electronegative than fluorine, so it attracts the shared electrons more strongly.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: The Assertion is true: F is −1, so O is +2. The Reason is false: fluorine is more electronegative than oxygen, and this is why oxygen is positive — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** When silver nitrate solution is added to sodium chloride solution, silver is reduced to silver metal.

**Reason (R):** In the product silver chloride, the oxidation number of silver is 0.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both statements are false. Ag is +1 in silver nitrate and still +1 in AgCl, so no oxidation number changes and no reduction occurs; this is a precipitation reaction, not a redox reaction — option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Hydrogen peroxide can act both as an oxidising agent and as a reducing agent.

**Reason (R):** Oxygen in hydrogen peroxide has the oxidation number −1, which lies between −2 and 0.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both statements are true. Oxygen at −1 can fall to −2 (H₂O₂ oxidising) or rise to 0 (H₂O₂ reducing), because −1 is intermediate; Reason explains Assertion — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** In acidic medium the permanganate ion is reduced to the manganese(II) ion.

**Reason (R):** Crystals of potassium permanganate are dark purple.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both statements are true, but the Reason is unrelated to the Assertion: the reduction product depends on the medium (Mn²⁺ in acid, MnO₂ in neutral or basic medium), not on the colour of the crystals — option (b).

questions.stem_md: True or false? The reaction of barium chloride solution with sodium sulphate solution, which gives a white precipitate of barium sulphate, is a redox reaction because a new solid is formed.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. Ba stays +2, S stays +6 and Cl stays −1; with no change in any oxidation number it is a precipitation reaction, not a redox reaction.

questions.stem_md: True or false? In the reduction half-reaction written for the ion-electron method, the electrons appear on the product side.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. In a reduction half-reaction electrons are gained, so they appear on the reactant (left) side; they appear on the right in an oxidation half-reaction.

questions.stem_md: True or false? The average oxidation number of sulphur in the tetrathionate ion S₄O₆²⁻ is +2.5, a fraction, because its sulphur atoms do not all have the same oxidation number.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: True. $4x + 6(-2) = -2$ gives $x = +2.5$ as an average; the S atoms are in two different environments, so the average is not a whole number.

questions.stem_md: The oxidation number of an atom in a free element, such as sulphur in S₈, is ___.
questions.solution_md: An atom in an uncombined element has oxidation number zero.

questions.stem_md: In the ion-electron method, in either acidic or basic medium, oxygen atoms are balanced by adding ___ molecules.
questions.solution_md: Oxygen is balanced with H₂O molecules; hydrogen is then balanced with H⁺ (acid) or OH⁻ (base).

questions.stem_md: The oxidation number of chlorine in the perchlorate ion, ClO₄⁻, is ___.
Match each reaction (column I) with its oxidising agent (column II).

options.text_md: 2Al + Fe₂O₃ → Al₂O₃ + 2Fe
Cl₂ + 2KI → 2KCl + I₂
Zn + 2H⁺ → Zn²⁺ + H₂
Cu + 2Ag⁺ → Cu²⁺ + 2Ag

questions.solution_md: The oxidising agent is the species that is reduced: Fe in Fe₂O₃ (+3 to 0), Cl₂ (0 to −1), H⁺ (+1 to 0) and Ag⁺ (+1 to 0).

questions.stem_md: Match each species or atom (column I) with its oxidation number (column II).

options.text_md: Cr in K₂Cr₂O₇
S in S₂O₃²⁻
Average S in Na₂S₄O₆
O in H₂O₂

questions.solution_md: K₂Cr₂O₇: +6; S₂O₃²⁻: +2; Na₂S₄O₆: +2.5 (average); H₂O₂: oxygen −1 (peroxide).

questions.stem_md: In acidic solution the dichromate ion is reduced to chromium(III) ions. Calculate the number of electrons gained by one Cr₂O₇²⁻ ion.
questions.solution_md: Cr changes from $+6$ to $+3$: a fall of 3 per atom. There are 2 Cr atoms in $\ce{Cr2O7^2-}$, so electrons gained $= 2 \times 3 = 6$.

marking_scheme.step: Fall of 3 per Cr atom (+6 to +3)

questions.stem_md: A student in a quality-control laboratory must oxidise 0.0300 mol of Fe²⁺ in acidic solution with potassium dichromate (M = 294 g mol⁻¹). Calculate the mass of K₂Cr₂O₇ required, in grams.

questions.stem_md: In a physics-laboratory demonstration, a piece of potassium burns in bromine vapour: 2K + Br₂ → 2KBr. In terms of electron transfer, write the two half-reactions and name the substance that is oxidised and the oxidising agent.

answer.model_answer_md: Oxidation half: $\ce{K -> K+ + e-}$ (potassium loses an electron). Reduction half: $\ce{Br2 + 2e- -> 2Br-}$ (bromine gains electrons). Potassium is oxidised (it is the reducing agent); bromine is reduced, so bromine is the oxidising agent.

questions.solution_md: K → K⁺ + e⁻ (oxidised); Br₂ + 2e⁻ → 2Br⁻; Br₂ is the oxidising agent.

marking_scheme.step: Both half-reactions with electrons on the correct sides
Potassium oxidised; bromine is the oxidising agent

questions.stem_md: A metallurgy student heats black copper(II) oxide in a stream of hydrogen and obtains red copper and steam: CuO + H₂ → Cu + H₂O. Using the oxygen and hydrogen definitions, state which substance is oxidised and which is reduced, and name both agents.

answer.model_answer_md: Copper(II) oxide loses oxygen, so it is reduced and is the oxidising agent. Hydrogen gains oxygen (it forms water), so it is oxidised and is the reducing agent.

questions.solution_md: CuO loses oxygen: reduced, oxidising agent. H₂ gains oxygen: oxidised, reducing agent.

marking_scheme.step: CuO reduced (loss of oxygen) and H₂ oxidised (gain of oxygen)
CuO is the oxidising agent and H₂ the reducing agent

questions.stem_md: Oxygen has the oxidation number −2 in most of its compounds. State its oxidation number in (a) hydrogen peroxide and (b) oxygen difluoride, with the reason in each case.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) In $\ce{H2O2}$ there is an O–O bond, and H is $+1$: $2(+1) + 2x = 0$, so $x = −1$ (peroxide). (b) In $\ce{OF2}$ fluorine is more electronegative than oxygen and is $-1$: $x + 2(-1) = 0$, so $x = +2$.

questions.solution_md: H₂O₂: O is −1 (peroxide); OF₂: O is +2 (F is more electronegative).

marking_scheme.step: (a) −1 with the sum equation or the O–O bond

questions.stem_md: Magnetite, Fe₃O₄, is the black magnetic ore of iron. Calculate the average oxidation number of iron in it, and show that the value fits a mixture of Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺ ions in the ratio 1 : 2.

answer.model_answer_md: $3x + 4(-2) = 0$, so $x = \dfrac{8}{3} = +2.67$ (average). A mixture of one $\ce{Fe^2+}$ and two $\ce{Fe^3+}$ gives $(2 + 3 + 3)/3 = 8/3$, the same average.

questions.solution_md: Average ON of Fe = +8/3 = +2.67, equal to (2 + 3 + 3)/3.

questions.stem_md: A student adds tin(II) chloride solution to a yellow solution of iron(III) chloride until the colour fades: 2FeCl₃ + SnCl₂ → 2FeCl₂ + SnCl₄. Using oxidation numbers, show that this is a redox reaction and name the reducing agent.

answer.model_answer_md: Fe falls from $+3$ to $+2$ (reduced); Sn rises from $+2$ to $+4$ (oxidised); Cl stays $-1$. Because oxidation numbers change, it is a redox reaction, and tin(II) chloride (Sn²⁺), which is oxidised, is the reducing agent.

questions.solution_md: Fe +3 → +2, Sn +2 → +4: redox; SnCl₂ is the reducing agent.

questions.stem_md: A chemistry teacher neutralises dilute nitric acid with potassium hydroxide: HNO₃ + KOH → KNO₃ + H₂O. Write the oxidation number of every element on the two sides and say whether the reaction is a redox reaction.

answer.model_answer_md: H $+1$ on both sides, N $+5$ on both sides, O $-2$ on both sides and K $+1$ on both sides. No oxidation number changes, so it is not a redox reaction.

questions.solution_md: H +1, N +5, O −2, K +1 on both sides: not redox.

marking_scheme.step: Oxidation numbers H +1, N +5, O −2, K +1 on both sides
No change, so not a redox reaction

questions.stem_md: State the two conditions that a correctly balanced ionic redox equation must satisfy. Why do free electrons not appear in the final equation?

answer.model_answer_md: The atoms of every element must be equal on both sides, and the total charge must be equal on both sides (the electrons lost by the reducing agent equal those gained by the oxidising agent, so the total rise in oxidation number equals the total fall). Electrons are cancelled when the two half-reactions are added, because those lost in the oxidation half are exactly those gained in the reduction half.

questions.solution_md: Atoms and charge balance; the electrons cancel between the two halves.

marking_scheme.step: Atoms and total charge equal on both sides
Electrons lost equal electrons gained, so they cancel on adding the halves

questions.stem_md: Classify each reaction as combination, decomposition, displacement or disproportionation, with the oxidation number evidence: (a) PCl₃ + Cl₂ → PCl₅; (b) 2NaNO₃ → 2NaNO₂ + O₂ on strong heating.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Combination: two substances give one; P rises from $+3$ to $+5$ and Cl falls from 0 to $-1$. (b) Decomposition: one compound gives two substances; N falls from $+5$ to $+3$ and O rises from $-2$ to 0, so it is also a redox reaction.

questions.solution_md: (a) combination (P +3 → +5, Cl 0 → −1); (b) decomposition (N +5 → +3, O −2 → 0).

questions.stem_md: Balance the half-reaction MnO₄⁻ → MnO₂ (basic medium) by the ion-electron method, and state the number of electrons gained by one MnO₄⁻ ion. This is a skeletal half-reaction.

answer.model_answer_md: Mn falls from $+7$ to $+4$. Balance O with water: $\ce{MnO4- -> MnO2 + 2H2O}$; balance H with $\ce{H+}$ and then turn them into water with $\ce{OH-}$ (basic medium). Balance the charge with electrons: $\ce{MnO4- + 2H2O + 3e- -> MnO2 + 4OH-}$. Three electrons are gained.

questions.solution_md: MnO₄⁻ + 2H₂O + 3e⁻ → MnO₂ + 4OH⁻: three electrons.

marking_scheme.step: Balances O and H with H₂O and OH⁻ (basic medium)
Balances charge: 3e⁻ on the left of MnO₄⁻ + 2H₂O → MnO₂ + 4OH⁻

questions.stem_md: For each reaction, identify the substance oxidised, the substance reduced and the reducing agent, quoting the oxidation numbers: (a) 2Mg + CO₂ → 2MgO + C; (b) Cu + 2Ag⁺ → Cu²⁺ + 2Ag; (c) Cu + 2H₂SO₄ → CuSO₄ + SO₂ + 2H₂O (hot, concentrated acid).

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Mg rises $0 \to +2$ (oxidised, the reducing agent); C falls $+4 \to 0$ (CO₂ is reduced). (b) Cu rises $0 \to +2$ (oxidised, the reducing agent); Ag⁺ falls $+1 \to 0$ (reduced). (c) Cu rises $0 \to +2$ (oxidised, the reducing agent); S falls from $+6$ in H₂SO₄ to $+4$ in SO₂ (the acid is reduced).

questions.solution_md: Mg, Cu and Cu are oxidised (reducing agents); CO₂, Ag⁺ and H₂SO₄ are reduced.

questions.stem_md: A fertiliser chemist compares three nitrogen compounds. Calculate the oxidation number of nitrogen in (a) the ammonium ion, NH₄⁺, (b) sodium nitrite, NaNO₂, and (c) nitric acid, HNO₃.
questions.solution_md: N is −3 in NH₄⁺, +3 in NaNO₂ and +5 in HNO₃.

questions.stem_md: Sodium tetrathionate, Na₂S₄O₆, is formed when thiosulphate is oxidised by iodine. Calculate the average oxidation number of sulphur in the S₄O₆²⁻ ion and explain why it is not a whole number. In the ion the two middle sulphur atoms carry no oxygen and the two end sulphur atoms each carry three oxygen atoms; state the oxidation number of each kind of sulphur atom.

answer.model_answer_md: $4x + 6(-2) = -2$, so $x = +2.5$ (average). The sulphur atoms are not all alike, so the oxidation number is an average. Each end SO₃ group is a unit of charge $-1$: $x + 3(-2) = -1$, so each end S is $+5$; the two middle S atoms (bonded only to sulphur) are 0. Check: $(5 + 5 + 0 + 0)/4 = 2.5$.

questions.solution_md: Average +2.5; end S atoms +5, middle S atoms 0.

marking_scheme.step: A fraction is an average over atoms in different environments
End S = +5 and middle S = 0, with the check (5 + 5 + 0 + 0)/4

questions.stem_md: Zinc reduces very dilute nitric acid to the ammonium ion. Balance the skeletal equation Zn + NO₃⁻ → Zn²⁺ + NH₄⁺ (acidic medium) by the oxidation number method.

answer.model_answer_md: Zn rises from 0 to $+2$ (rise 2); N falls from $+5$ to $-3$ (fall 8). Total rise = total fall needs 4 Zn per N: $\ce{4Zn + NO3- -> 4Zn^2+ + NH4+}$. Charge: left $-1$, right $+9$, so add $10\ \ce{H+}$ on the left. O: 3 on the left, so $3\ \ce{H2O}$ on the right, and H is then 10 on each side: $\ce{4Zn + NO3- + 10H+ -> 4Zn^2+ + NH4+ + 3H2O}$.

questions.solution_md: 4Zn + NO₃⁻ + 10H⁺ → 4Zn²⁺ + NH₄⁺ + 3H₂O.

marking_scheme.step: Zn rise 2, N fall 8, so 4 Zn per N
Charge balanced with 10 H⁺ on the left
3 H₂O on the right and the check of atoms and charge

questions.stem_md: A chemist titrates iodide ions with acidified dichromate. Balance the skeletal equation Cr₂O₇²⁻ + I⁻ → Cr³⁺ + I₂ (acidic medium) by the ion-electron method.

answer.model_answer_md: Reduction: $\ce{Cr2O7^2- + 14H+ + 6e- -> 2Cr^3+ + 7H2O}$. Oxidation: $\ce{2I- -> I2 + 2e-}$. Multiply the oxidation half by 3 to equalise the 6 electrons and add: $\ce{Cr2O7^2- + 14H+ + 6I- -> 2Cr^3+ + 7H2O + 3I2}$. Charge: $-2 + 14 - 6 = +6$ and $2(+3) = +6$.

questions.solution_md: Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 14H⁺ + 6I⁻ → 2Cr³⁺ + 7H₂O + 3I₂.

marking_scheme.step: Final equation with the charge check +6 on each side

questions.stem_md: Permanganate oxidises oxalate ions in basic medium, giving manganese dioxide and carbonate ions. Balance the skeletal equation MnO₄⁻ + C₂O₄²⁻ → MnO₂ + CO₃²⁻ (basic medium) by the ion-electron method.

answer.model_answer_md: Reduction: $\ce{MnO4- + 2H2O + 3e- -> MnO2 + 4OH-}$. Oxidation: $\ce{C2O4^2- + 4OH- -> 2CO3^2- + 2H2O + 2e-}$. Multiply the reduction half by 2 and the oxidation half by 3 (6 electrons) and add; cancel 4 H₂O and 8 OH⁻ that appear on both sides: $\ce{3C2O4^2- + 2MnO4- + 4OH- -> 6CO3^2- + 2MnO2 + 2H2O}$. Charge: $-6 - 2 - 4 = -12$ on the left and $-12$ on the right.

questions.solution_md: 3C₂O₄²⁻ + 2MnO₄⁻ + 4OH⁻ → 6CO₃²⁻ + 2MnO₂ + 2H₂O.

marking_scheme.step: Multipliers 2 and 3, cancellation and the final equation with charge −12

questions.stem_md: Identify the type of each reaction, with the change in oxidation number as evidence: (a) 2Al + Fe₂O₃ → Al₂O₃ + 2Fe; (b) 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂; (c) CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂ (say whether it is a redox reaction at all).

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Displacement: Al rises $0 \to +3$ and Fe falls $+3 \to 0$ (aluminium displaces iron). (b) Decomposition that is also disproportionation: oxygen at $-1$ falls to $-2$ in H₂O and rises to 0 in O₂. (c) Decomposition that is not redox: Ca $+2$, C $+4$ and O $-2$ are unchanged.

questions.solution_md: (a) displacement; (b) disproportionation (O −1 → −2 and 0); (c) decomposition, not redox.

marking_scheme.step: (c) Not redox: no oxidation number changes

questions.stem_md: A student balances the skeletal equation MnO₄⁻ + Fe²⁺ → Mn²⁺ + Fe³⁺ in acid as MnO₄⁻ + Fe²⁺ + 8H⁺ → Mn²⁺ + Fe³⁺ + 4H₂O, and finds that Mn, Fe, O and H all balance. Show by counting charge that the equation is wrong, and give the correct equation with the reason.

answer.model_answer_md: Charge on the left: $-1 + 2 + 8 = +9$; on the right: $+2 + 3 = +5$. The charges differ, so the equation is wrong. Mn falls by 5 while each Fe rises by 1, so 5 Fe²⁺ are needed per MnO₄⁻ to make total rise equal total fall: $\ce{MnO4- + 8H+ + 5Fe^2+ -> Mn^2+ + 4H2O + 5Fe^3+}$ (charge $+17$ on each side).

questions.solution_md: Charge +9 on the left but +5 on the right; correct: MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5Fe²⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O + 5Fe³⁺.

marking_scheme.step: Charge +9 on the left against +5 on the right
Mn falls by 5, Fe rises by 1, so 5 Fe²⁺ are needed
Correct equation with charge +17 on each side

questions.stem_md: Hydrogen peroxide acts as an oxidising agent towards iron(II) ions in acid, but as a reducing agent towards chlorine. Using oxidation numbers, explain why it can do both, and write one equation for each action.

answer.model_answer_md: Oxygen in H₂O₂ is $-1$, which lies between $-2$ (in water or oxides) and 0 (in O₂), so it can fall or rise. As an oxidising agent oxygen falls to $-2$: $\ce{2Fe^2+ + H2O2 + 2H+ -> 2Fe^3+ + 2H2O}$. As a reducing agent oxygen rises to 0: $\ce{H2O2 + Cl2 -> 2HCl + O2}$.

questions.solution_md: O is −1 (intermediate); 2Fe²⁺ + H₂O₂ + 2H⁺ → 2Fe³⁺ + 2H₂O; H₂O₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl + O₂.

marking_scheme.step: O at −1 lies between −2 and 0, so it can be reduced or oxidised
Oxidising action with a balanced equation (O −1 → −2)
Reducing action with a balanced equation (O −1 → 0)

questions.stem_md: A pharmacy laboratory oxidises 1.26 g of sodium sulphite, Na₂SO₃ (M = 126 g mol⁻¹), in acid with 0.0200 M potassium permanganate; permanganate is reduced to Mn²⁺ and sulphite becomes sulphate. (a) From the changes in oxidation number, show that 2 mol of MnO₄⁻ oxidise 5 mol of SO₃²⁻. (b) Calculate the volume of the permanganate solution needed, in mL.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Mn falls from $+7$ to $+2$ (fall 5); S rises from $+4$ to $+6$ (rise 2). Total rise = total fall: $2 \times 5 = 5 \times 2$, so 2 MnO₄⁻ react with 5 SO₃²⁻. (b) $n(\ce{SO3^2-}) = 1.26/126 = 0.0100$ mol; $n(\ce{MnO4-}) = \tfrac25 \times 0.0100 = 0.0040$ mol; $V = 0.0040/0.0200 = 0.200$ L $= 200$ mL.

questions.solution_md: 200 mL of permanganate.

marking_scheme.step: (a) Mn falls by 5, S rises by 2, so the ratio is 2 : 5

questions.stem_md:
Chromium(III) hydroxide is oxidised by chlorate ions in basic solution to chromate ions, and the chlorate ion is reduced to chloride ions. The skeletal equation is Cr(OH)₃ + ClO₃⁻ → CrO₄²⁻ + Cl⁻ (basic medium).

(a) Find the oxidation numbers of Cr and Cl on each side, the change per atom, and the ratio in which Cr(OH)₃ and ClO₃⁻ react. [2]

(b) Balance the equation by the oxidation number method, adding OH⁻ and H₂O where needed, and show that atoms and charge balance. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Cr in Cr(OH)₃: $x + 3(-1) = 0$, so $+3$; in CrO₄²⁻: $+6$ (rise 3 per Cr). Cl in ClO₃⁻: $+5$; in Cl⁻: $-1$ (fall 6 per Cl). Total rise = total fall needs 2 Cr for each Cl, so $\ce{Cr(OH)3}$ : $\ce{ClO3-}$ $= 2 : 1$.

(b) $\ce{2Cr(OH)3 + ClO3- -> 2CrO4^2- + Cl-}$. Charge: left $-1$, right $-4 - 1 = -5$, so add $4\ \ce{OH-}$ on the left. H: left $6 + 4 = 10$, so $5\ \ce{H2O}$ on the right. $\ce{2Cr(OH)3 + ClO3- + 4OH- -> 2CrO4^2- + Cl- + 5H2O}$. Check: Cr 2, Cl 1, O $6 + 3 + 4 = 13 = 8 + 5$, H $6 + 4 = 10 = 10$; charge $-5$ on each side.

questions.solution_md: 2Cr(OH)₃ + ClO₃⁻ + 4OH⁻ → 2CrO₄²⁻ + Cl⁻ + 5H₂O.

marking_scheme.step: (b) Balances charge with 4 OH⁻ on the left
(b) Balances H and O with 5 H₂O on the right
(b) Final equation with the check of atoms and charge (−5 on each side)

questions.stem_md:
Acidified permanganate oxidises oxalate ions to carbon dioxide. The skeletal equation is MnO₄⁻ + C₂O₄²⁻ → Mn²⁺ + CO₂ (acidic medium).

(a) Write the balanced oxidation half-reaction and the balanced reduction half-reaction. [2]

(b) Equalise the electrons and write the balanced ionic equation. [2]

(c) Show that the charge is balanced in your equation. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Oxidation: $\ce{C2O4^2- -> 2CO2 + 2e-}$. Reduction: $\ce{MnO4- + 8H+ + 5e- -> Mn^2+ + 4H2O}$.

(b) Multiply the oxidation half by 5 and the reduction half by 2 (10 electrons each) and add: $\ce{5C2O4^2- + 2MnO4- + 16H+ -> 10CO2 + 2Mn^2+ + 8H2O}$.

(c) Charge on the left: $5(-2) + 2(-1) + 16 = +4$. Charge on the right: $2(+2) = +4$ (CO₂ and H₂O are neutral). Atoms also balance: C 10, O 28, Mn 2, H 16.

questions.solution_md: 5C₂O₄²⁻ + 2MnO₄⁻ + 16H⁺ → 10CO₂ + 2Mn²⁺ + 8H₂O.

marking_scheme.step: (b) Multipliers 5 and 2 so that 10 electrons cancel

questions.stem_md:
A pharmacist checks a bottle of hydrogen peroxide by titration. A 20.0 mL sample is acidified and needs 16.0 mL of 0.0200 M potassium permanganate to reach the end point. The balanced equation is 2MnO₄⁻ + 5H₂O₂ + 6H⁺ → 2Mn²⁺ + 5O₂ + 8H₂O.

(a) State the change in oxidation number of manganese and of oxygen, and name the oxidising agent and the reducing agent. [2]

(b) Calculate the molarity of the hydrogen peroxide solution. [2]

(c) Calculate its concentration in g L⁻¹ (M = 34 g mol⁻¹). [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Mn falls from $+7$ to $+2$; O in H₂O₂ rises from $-1$ to 0. Permanganate is the oxidising agent (it is reduced) and hydrogen peroxide is the reducing agent (it is oxidised).

(b) $n(\ce{MnO4-}) = 0.0160 \times 0.0200 = 3.20\times10^{-4}$ mol. From the equation $n(\ce{H2O2}) = \tfrac52 \times 3.20\times10^{-4} = 8.00\times10^{-4}$ mol in 0.0200 L, so $c = 8.00\times10^{-4}/0.0200 = 0.0400$ mol L⁻¹.

(c) Mass concentration $= 0.0400 \times 34 = 1.36$ g L⁻¹.

questions.solution_md: c = 0.0400 mol per litre, 1.36 g per litre.

marking_scheme.step: (a) Permanganate is the oxidising agent and H₂O₂ the reducing agent

questions.stem_md:
Nitrous acid is unstable in solution and changes to nitric acid and nitrogen monoxide: 3HNO₂ → HNO₃ + 2NO + H₂O.

(a) Define disproportionation. [1]

(b) Using oxidation numbers, show that this reaction is a disproportionation and that the electrons lost equal the electrons gained. [2]

(c) Explain why nitrous acid can disproportionate but nitric acid cannot. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) A redox reaction in which the same element in one substance is both oxidised and reduced.

(b) N in HNO₂ is $+3$. In HNO₃ it is $+5$ (rise 2, one N atom lost 2 electrons). In NO it is $+2$ (fall 1 per N, two N atoms gain 2 electrons). The same element rises and falls, and $2 = 2$ electrons lost and gained.

(c) N in HNO₂ is at $+3$, an intermediate value between its highest $+5$ and lower values, so it can rise to $+5$ and fall to $+2$. In HNO₃ nitrogen is already at its highest oxidation number $+5$, so it can only fall (be reduced) and cannot also rise.

questions.solution_md: Same element oxidised and reduced; N +3 → +5 and +2; HNO₃ has N at its maximum +5.

marking_scheme.step: (a) Same element simultaneously oxidised and reduced
(b) N +3 → +5 (rise 2) and N +3 → +2 (fall 1 for each of two N)
(c) HNO₂: N at intermediate +3 can rise and fall
(c) HNO₃: N at the highest +5 can only fall

questions.stem_md:
A student studies three reactions: (i) CaO + H₂O → Ca(OH)₂; (ii) 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO; (iii) 2Na₂S₂O₃ + I₂ → Na₂S₄O₆ + 2NaI.

(a) State, with oxidation numbers, which of the three are redox reactions. [3]

(b) For reaction (iii), name the oxidising agent and the reducing agent and give the oxidation number of sulphur on each side. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) (i) Ca $+2$, O $-2$ and H $+1$ on both sides: no change, so not redox. (ii) Mg rises $0 \to +2$ and O falls $0 \to -2$: redox. (iii) S rises from $+2$ to $+2.5$ (average) and I falls from 0 to $-1$: redox.

(b) Iodine is reduced, so I₂ is the oxidising agent; thiosulphate is oxidised, so S₂O₃²⁻ is the reducing agent. S is $+2$ in thiosulphate and an average of $+2.5$ in tetrathionate.

questions.solution_md: (ii) and (iii) are redox; I₂ oxidising agent, S₂O₃²⁻ reducing agent; S +2 → +2.5.

marking_scheme.step: (i) No oxidation number changes: not redox
(b) I₂ oxidising agent; S₂O₃²⁻ reducing agent
(b) S +2 on the left and +2.5 (average) on the right

questions.stem_md:
In basic solution aluminium reduces nitrate ions to ammonia, and the aluminium forms aluminate ions, AlO₂⁻. The skeletal equation is Al + NO₃⁻ → AlO₂⁻ + NH₃ (basic medium).

(a) Balance the oxidation half-reaction and the reduction half-reaction in basic medium. [3]

(b) Combine the two halves and give the final balanced equation, cancelling the species common to both sides. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Oxidation: $\ce{Al + 4OH- -> AlO2- + 2H2O + 3e-}$ (Al $0 \to +3$). Reduction: $\ce{NO3- + 6H2O + 8e- -> NH3 + 9OH-}$ (N $+5 \to -3$).

(b) Multiply the oxidation half by 8 and the reduction half by 3 (24 electrons each) and add: $\ce{8Al + 32OH- + 3NO3- + 18H2O -> 8AlO2- + 16H2O + 3NH3 + 27OH-}$. Cancel 16 H₂O and 27 OH⁻: $\ce{8Al + 5OH- + 3NO3- + 2H2O -> 8AlO2- + 3NH3}$. Charge: $-5 - 3 = -8$ on the left and $8(-1) = -8$ on the right.

questions.solution_md: 8Al + 5OH⁻ + 3NO₃⁻ + 2H₂O → 8AlO₂⁻ + 3NH₃.

marking_scheme.step: (b) Multipliers 8 and 3 so that 24 electrons cancel
